title: Scientist Jim Bruce was a globally renowned voice on the dangers of climate change
sourceDescription: A founding member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, he was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Scientist Jim Bruce was a globally renowned voice on the dangers of climate change James Cullingham Special to The Globe and Mail Published Yesterday Open this photo in gallery: Jim Bruce, who died on Aug. 23, was a founding member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. The Bruce family/Supplied

Jim Bruce was one of Canada’s foremost scientists and international representatives concerning environmental and climate issues. He provided extraordinary leadership that helped to rehabilitate the Great Lakes and through proposing the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was among the first to show how the world could address the damaging climate change caused by the burning of fossil fuels. He became a globally renowned and trusted voice who raised awareness about the risks of climate change, especially flooding and drought.

“If climate change is a shark, water is its teeth,” Mr. Bruce said, according to MP Francis Scarpaleggia, who quoted the scientist when addressing the House of Commons in 2022. “Like a fish that doesn’t notice the shark until it feels its sharp bite, humans will first feel the effects of climate change through water.”

Mr. Bruce, a leading member of the IPCC, was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore, who was honoured for his work on climate change, including the Oscar-winning film An Inconvenient Truth .

Jim Bruce died at the age of 97 in Ottawa on Aug. 23. He had suffered for many years from inclusion body myositis (IBM).

“[Mr. Bruce] was one of the first to raise and develop to prominence so many issues like floodplain mapping, hydrometeorology, the imperative to control climate change. There’s both a scientific and organizational legacy,” said John Pomeroy, distinguished professor at the University of Saskatchewan. “He showed us that Canada could be leaders in such matters. He was a great Canadian.”

Rower Archie MacKinnon helped usher in a golden age for his sport on Canada’s West Coast

James Philip Bruce was born in Toronto on Sept. 29, 1928. His father, Peter Bruce, worked in the shoe department at Eaton’s department store. His mother, Winnifred Bruce, was an elementary school teacher who left her job when she had children. She later continued her vocation as an English as second language instructor. As a young person, Jim accompanied his father, a tenor vocalist, on piano and organ at church services.

Mr. Bruce received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Toronto in 1948. That year he began a career at the Meteorological Service of Canada working mostly at air force bases. In 1949 he married Ruth (née Richardson), to whom he was married for 77 years. In 1952, Mr. Bruce went back to the University of Toronto and earned a master’s degree in physics.

The devastation of Hurricane Hazel in 1954 was a pivotal moment in his understanding of climate. He did floodplain mapping which led to the mitigation of future risk in the immediate area of the Humber River in Toronto’s west end, where loss of life and extensive property damage had occurred, and elsewhere.

The aftermath of Hurricane Hazel on Oct. 18, 1954. The devastation wrought by Hazel was a pivotal moment in Mr. Bruce's understanding of climate. The Globe and Mail/The Globe and Mail

Mr. Bruce and others developed systems to prepare for and avoid risks of flooding in several parts of Canada. That work also led to the creation of park space around urban rivers. His son, Peter Bruce, a former senior civil servant and now a learning and leadership associate at the Institute on Governance, a think tank, posed the query: “Do you know why it’s green around the Don Valley Parkway [in Toronto]? It’s because of my father.”

He was head of hydrometeorology for the Meteorological Service of Canada, based in Toronto, from 1959 to 1967. Mr. Bruce then moved to Burlington, Ont., where he led the Centre for Inland Waters and became co-chair of the International Joint Commission (IJC), dedicated to protection of water quality of the Great Lakes. That was the beginning of a series of international roles that saw Mr. Bruce involved with IPCC and the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva.

In 1988, he helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto titled “The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security.” That gathering marked the first time a global conference called for a reduction – 20 per cent – in greenhouse gas emissions. Mr. Bruce helped write the conference statement, which began: “Humanity is conducting an unintended, uncontrolled, globally pervasive experiment whose ultimate consequences could be second only to a global nuclear war.”

Following that Toronto conference, Mr. Bruce was among an international team that formed the IPCC. This body provides scientific assessments that inform decision-makers at United Nations climate conferences, known as Conferences of the Parties (COPs), and has helped shape international agreements including the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Mr. Bruce reflected on his IPCC experience in his 2016 book A Canadian Environmental Chronicle (1954-2015) . “While many climate activists have rightly considered IPCC Reports to be cautious in tone, this characteristic is inevitable in reports that represent a consensus of a large, diverse, international group of scientists,” he wrote.

In a 2022 interview with John Woodside for Canada’s National Observer, Mr. Bruce signalled his growing dissatisfaction on the climate-change mitigation front: “Now it [the IPCC] hasn’t been very successful in getting real action, in my view, but that’s a political problem.”

Public awareness, however, has grown. Mr. Bruce wrote about the moment he and his colleagues returned to their hotel after the Nobel Peace Prize gala: “We were astonished to find a large crowd waiting for our return from the ceremony. They began shouting ‘I-P-C-C, I-P-C-C’ and continued for some time. In my experience, this only happened to winning sports teams.”

Filmmaker Georgina Lightning set out to change how Indigenous people were seen and heard

His daughter Cathy Bruce, president and vice-chancellor of Trent University, laughingly recalled chatting with her father before he headed to Oslo: “He asked, ‘Do you think I should rent a suit?’ I said, ‘Dad, maybe this is a time you should buy a new suit.’” Dr. Bruce said she tries to implement her father’s style in valuing mentoring and in striving to make complex ideas understandable both in speech and writing.

Dr. Pomeroy first met Mr. Bruce in 1981 at the University of Saskatchewan. “I was a 20-year-old undergraduate asked to drive to the airport to pick up this leading figure. I was terrified. It turns out he was a nice, humble person who immediately put me at ease.”

Earlier this month, Dr. Pomeroy was among the scientists who honoured Mr. Bruce at the World Climate Research Programme’s International Network for Alpine Research Catchment Hydrology meeting in Kananaskis, Alta.

Mr. Bruce’s scientific output alone is a significant legacy, Dr. Pomeroy said, pointing to a breakthrough 1965 text on hydrometeorology and the instrumentation embedded by Mr. Bruce’s team in the Canadian Rockies headwaters of the Bow River in the early 1960s that helped scientists later understand the causes of the massive floods of 2013 and how better to predict such events.

Elizabeth Dowdeswell, former lieutenant-governor of Ontario, met Mr. Bruce in the 1980s when they both worked for the federal government. She came from behavioural sciences rather than a meteorological or hydrological background.

“He was always there for you, teaching in the most gentle way. He was a mentor,” Ms. Dowdeswell said, adding that she felt welcomed by Mr. Bruce. She would assume senior roles at Canada’s Atmospheric Environmental Service and as head of the United Nations Environment Programme in Nairobi, Kenya. She fondly recalled an interaction early in her Ottawa stint when she was “flabbergasted” by the number of acronyms used in the governmental scientific reports. “I told Jim I was determined to write a report without acronyms. Jim said, ‘good luck with that!’”

In 1988, Mr. Bruce helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto that called for a 20 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. John Evans/Supplied

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May, formerly an activist and environmental lawyer, first encountered Mr. Bruce after she became an adviser to Thomas McMillan, then federal minister of the environment, and through the intense period of the 1988 Toronto conference, after which Ms. May resigned from the minister’s office. Their relationship deepened from 1999 to 2005 when they both served on the board of the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD).

Ms. May admired Mr. Bruce’s ability to engage with diverse colleagues and to make complex scientific issues understandable. Mr. Bruce “was a kind of polymath,” she said. “He had moral courage, mental clarity and depth of scientific expertise. I relied on him and loved him enormously.”

Jim and Ruth Bruce led an active, engaged family life. As long as his health permitted, Mr. Bruce played both jazz and European classical on the piano. He particularly admired Oscar Peterson, Diana Krall and J.S. Bach. Both Cathy Bruce and her brother, Peter, remember music and travel as indelible parts of family life.

“My father took us on lots of adventures,” Peter recalled. “He was very interested in archaeology and history.” Skiing also figured at a family chalet at Mont Sainte-Marie in the Gatineau region and in the Alps when members of the extended family visited Jim and Ruth while they were stationed in Geneva.

Ms. May made a point of regularly dropping by Jim and Ruth Bruce’s condo overlooking the Ottawa River. Her most recent visit took place last winter. “Jim never lost hold of moral certainty based on clear evidence and science.” She recalled that even with his deteriorating medical condition, “I never heard a syllable that could amount to self-pity. He grabbed every moment to get all the joy from life that he could.”

Both Ms. May and Ms. Dowdeswell said their final conversations with Mr. Bruce included discussion of climate change. Mr. Bruce was particularly alarmed about Canadian backsliding, Ms. May said. “We were both angry to the point of tears.”

After leaving the federal civil service and WMO, Mr. Bruce remained engaged with writing, speaking at conferences and advising on domestic and international panels. He expressed mounting concern over what he saw as insufficient action on the environment.

“One of the long-standing requirements of government,” he wrote in his 2016 book, “is to ensure stewardship of our inherited land, air, water and wild creatures – to pass them largely unharmed to the next generation. This role has recently been abysmally short-changed.”

Before that book was published, Peter had expressed concern that the conclusion his father drafted might be too dire, so he advised his father to tone it down a bit, which he did. But more recently, upon reflection, Peter thought, “Well, Dad, I guess you were right again.”

Among his many honours, Jim Bruce was named an officer of the Order of Canada and Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1997, was awarded honorary doctorates from McMaster and Waterloo universities as well as being a member of the IPCC delegation for the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

Mr. Bruce leaves his wife, Ruth; children, Peggy Marcoux, Peter Bruce, Connie Bruce and Cathy Bruce; eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

title: Nova Scotia government spent nearly $2-billion outside of budget
sourceDescription: Province closed 2025-26 fiscal year with record-high deficit of $1.4-billion, Finance Minister says
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Nova Scotia government spent nearly $2-billion outside of budget Lyndsay Armstrong Halifax The Canadian Press Published Yesterday Open this photo in gallery: Nova Scotia Finance Minister John Lohr at a news conference providing a financial update in Halifax on Thursday. HO/The Canadian Press

The Nova Scotia government says it spent a record $1.9-billion more than what the provincial legislature had approved for the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Finance Minister John Lohr said there are plenty of reasons why the Progressive Conservative government spent so much money on what the government describes as additional appropriations.

“We need to be flexible as a government, and we will continue to do that,” he said during a news conference Thursday.

Additional appropriations refer to extra spending that is not included in the budget, but is approved by cabinet without a vote in the legislature.

The province’s auditor general has repeatedly called for stronger oversight on how the government spends money not included in the budget.

Lohr said much of the additional spending in the most recent fiscal year went to health care services and seniors.

The government also used some of that additional funding to cover the $40.4-million cost of public works projects and another $13.8-million on emergency management for the 2025 wildfire season.

The Department of Finance also said the increased spending includes $420-million in funds that were set aside for some anticipated commitments which have not yet been finalized and, as a result, cannot be made public.

Lohr would not say if this was related to a previous government’s wage restriction bill that was deemed unconstitutional.

Bill 148 was passed by former Liberal premier Stephen McNeil to limit pay increases in 2015, and a Supreme Court judge decided it was unconstitutional in February.

“In terms of Bill 148, I can say that we have until February of this coming year to reach a settlement, we are working on that,” Lohr said.

Officials declined to comment on how much this settlement may cost, because the matter is before the courts.

The province closed the 2025-26 fiscal year with a record-high deficit of $1.4-billion. While revenue was slightly higher than expected, at just under $18-billion, it was outpaced by $19.4-billion in spending.

For the 2026-27 fiscal year, the province is anticipating a $1.44-billion deficit.

Opposition parties slammed the Progressive Conservative government for its growing deficit and reliance on out-of-budget spending.

Interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin said Thursday’s update highlights the government’s inability to manage spending.

“We see a dozen departments, again, overspending and not going to the legislature to get approval. This is a government that loves to spend and there’s no accountability on the spending,” Rankin told reporters.

NDP finance critic, Lisa Lachance, said the province needs to look critically at its spending.

“This government has dug a generational hole for Nova Scotians in terms of deficit spending, debt, debt servicing costs. And yet people still aren’t getting what they need,” Lachance said.

The NDP member said the province continues to deal with crises in health care and affordable housing, despite significant government spending.

Lohr said Nova Scotians remain concerned about affordability, housing, health and seniors’ care, and the government has focused on spending in these areas.

“There are still so many things we want to do for Nova Scotians, and to do that we need to grow our economy. I believe we have the fundamentals required for growth in defence, in clean energy, in housing, and in natural resources,” the finance minister said.

title: Why Canada's rolling out the red carpet for Vietnamese President Tô Lâm
sourceDescription: Vietnam and Canada can deepen their relationships on trade, energy and academia, say experts — but some say the Southeast Asian country's track record on human rights shouldn't be ignored.
sourceBodyText:
Listen to this article Estimated 4 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Vietnamese President Tô Lâm, pictured here in May 2026, is paying a state visit to Canada in what could be a turning point for the two countries' relations. (Edgar Su/Reuters) Social Sharing From a welcoming ceremony with military honours to a lavish state dinner — as far as diplomatic events go, a state visit is as formal as it gets: the ultimate symbol of friendly bilateral relations.

Today, Canada will be greeting Vietnam's Tô Lâm with such a warm gesture. Lâm — who serves both as the president and the first general secretary of Vietnam's Communist Party — will be welcomed by Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour and Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a moment that could be a turning point for Canada-Vietnam relations.

The Southeast Asian country is a major trading partner, reaching $20.6 billion in two-way trade 2025. But it also has a checkered human rights record and keeps in good standing with adversaries like Russia and North Korea.

So why has Canada chosen its leader for its first state visit of 2026? CBC News spoke with several experts ahead of the occasion on what Canada stands to gain from closer ties to Vietnam.

In some ways, Canada and Vietnam have much in common: Both countries are middle powers, sharing a border with juggernauts (the U.S. and China, respectively).

Both nations have also been steadily increasing their bilateral trade in recent years — Vietnam is now Canada's largest trading partner in Southeast Asia.

Carney's Davos speech draws reaction from around the world

"Canada and Vietnam have had a comprehensive partnership since 2017," said Julie Nguyen, chair of the Canada-ASEAN Initiatives at the York Centre for Asian Research, referencing industries like trade, defence, science and diplomacy.

"It is time for the two countries to elevate their partnership to the next level in order to ensure economic resiliency, security."

Vietnam is racing to become a high-income country by 2045 . In order to reach that goal, it will have to move into advanced manufacturing, science, technology and AI development, Nguyen says.

Carney hosts investment summit amid trade war

September 13 | Duration closed caption 2:44 Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting a two day investment summit in Toronto in an attempt to attract foreign capital to the country amid an escalating trade war with the United States. "All of these products and services can be provided by Canada."

Canada is also working to finalize a free trade agreement with the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN). Vietnam could prove clutch in those efforts, since it is a prominent member of the intergovernmental regional organization, says Jeff Nankivell, president and CEO of the non-profit think-tank, the Asia Pacific Foundation.

And, Nankivell says, Canada is likely to find a willing partner in Vietnam, which has also faced punishing American tariffs, with the U.S. at one point slapping a 40 per cent levy on goods determined to have been transshipped through Vietnam.

"Everyone in the world is looking to diversify," he said.

"When we knock on the door of a country like Vietnam, it opens very quickly because they have a similar interest in diversifying."

Vietnam is also hungry for energy. It's one of the fastest-growing economies in the world and its population is relatively young and well educated .

That's of interest to Canada, because it could provide commodities like liquefied natural gas (LNG), says Nankivell.

Could Canada fill the Iran war oil supply gaps?

March 4 | Duration closed caption 2:02 With the Iran war threatening to upend much of the world's oil and gas supply from Gulf states, experts say there could be a big uptick in demand for Canadian energy products, but Canada's limited ability to get the products to market could be an obstacle. "On conventional energy, LNG and crude oil, there could be statements of intention on the Vietnamese side to look to Canada for future supplies," he said.

How Carney's Davos speech holds up 3 months later

Canada could also respond to Vietnam's ambitious nuclear power program, says Nankivell.

"You might see announcements or memoranda of understanding related to closer co-operation to explore the deployment or acquisition of Canadian nuclear technology in Vietnam."

But Canada and Vietnam also have key differences in values. Human Rights Watch highlighted this in an open letter addressed to Carney and Arbour about Vietnam's crackdown on political dissidents.

Amnesty International has accused Lâm's government of using a vague penal code to crack down on dissent and suppress freedom of expression.

He has also travelled to North Korea as recently as October of last year, a country with a dismal human rights record and from which Canada has suspended full diplomatic relations since 2010. Lâm has also held high-level talks earlier this month at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Vietnam's human rights record and allies, including a co-operative relationship with Russia, are points for Canada to consider in pursuing closer ties with the Southeast Asian country. (Maxim Shipenkov/AFP/Getty Images) Nankivell says it's an important reminder — and stronger trader relationships will only help Canada have more leverage in advancing liberal values.

Trump to hit more than 60 countries, including Canada, with new tariffs over 'forced labour'

"It is still very much in Canada's national interest to continue working towards a world where human rights are better respected than they are today, but you need channels for that," he said.

"Having a state visit with the leader of a country like Vietnam is an opportunity to deepen those ties."

title: Justice Minister Fraser orders court to revisit Indigenous sisters’ 1994 murder convictions
sourceDescription: Odelia and Neressa Quewezance have maintained their innocence and have spent almost three decades in prison
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Justice Minister Fraser orders court to revisit Indigenous sisters’ 1994 murder convictions Willow Fiddler Published 3 hours ago Open this photo in gallery: Odelia and Neressa Quewezance speak to media outside the Court of King's Bench in Yorkton, Sask., in March, 2023. Michael Bell/The Canadian Press

Two Indigenous sisters who have maintained their innocence since they were convicted of murder more than 30 years ago will have their case reviewed after federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser ordered a new appeal.

Mr. Fraser issued a statement that said an in-depth review had concluded that the 1994 convictions of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance were likely a “miscarriage of justice.”

The sisters have spent almost three decades in prison.

While Mr. Fraser cautioned that it is up to the courts, not him, to make findings of guilt or innocence, his department said new information was identified that had not been presented to the courts at the time of the sisters’ trial or appeal.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts for new information to be considered,” Mr. Fraser said in his statement.

From the archives: Indigenous sisters struggle to undo a 1994 murder conviction and break a cycle of parole and punishment

James Lockyer, the lawyer who represents the sisters on behalf of Innocence Canada, an advocacy group against wrongful convictions, said the new information is contained in the disclosure that the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal had to hand over to the Attorney-General but refused to give to the defence in the 1995 appeal case that was dismissed.

“We already had a basis for challenging the convictions but the new information that was provided by the Saskatchewan Attorney-General’s Office enhanced the strength of the application,” Mr. Lockyer told The Globe and Mail.

Odelia Quewezance made a statement through Innocence Canada on Thursday.

“Neressa was 18 when she was arrested and is now 52. I was 21 and am now 55. But we have never stopped fighting. Today’s announcement by the Minister is encouraging and now we will continue the fight in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal. Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

Neressa and Odelia were arrested and charged in the stabbing death of 70-year-old Joseph Dolff, a janitor at the local residential school that the sisters attended in their home community of Keeseekoose First Nation, Sask.

From the archives: Case of Indigenous sisters serving life sentence underscores need to reform review process for miscarriages of justice, lawyer says

The sisters’ 15-year-old male cousin, whose identity remains protected because he was a youth at the time, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and confessed to the crime.

He later testified at the sisters’ trial that he was the one who ultimately caused Mr. Dolff’s death at his farmhouse northeast of Kamsack, Sask., by tying a phone cord around his neck, throwing a television on him and stabbing him. He said the sisters only participated in the initial assault.

On the night of Feb. 25, 1993, the sisters had been drinking heavily, consuming significant quantities of beer and whisky provided to them by Mr. Dolff, who himself was not drinking. The sisters and their cousin also took prescription sleeping pills, both orally and by injection.

Court would later hear that at some point in the evening, Odelia took money from Mr. Dolff’s bedroom, and the group decided to leave.

Mr. Dolff was driving the sisters and their cousin home when he discovered the money was missing and they returned to his property. There, a violent confrontation ensued, in which Mr. Dolff was beaten, hit with household items and then stabbed to death.

The sisters and their cousin were arrested later that day.

From the archives: Saskatchewan judge orders release of sisters jailed for 30 years for a murder they say they didn’t commit

The sisters pleaded not guilty, but a jury found them guilty and a judge sentenced them to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years, the shortest period of parole eligibility possible for a murder sentence.

A ministerial review of the sisters’ conviction was granted in June of 2022, several months after Mr. Lockyer applied in a last bid for his clients’ freedom. The sisters were granted bail in 2023 before returning to custody for breaching release conditions.

The sisters’ time in custody, particularly in the days after their arrest by the RCMP has long been questioned by Mr. Lockyer and advocates.

Mr. Lockyer said the women’s alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and that as residential school survivors, they were more vulnerable to the pressures of police and of being in an in-custody environment that could have likely resulted in false confessions.

Innocence Canada called this week’s order of appeal a step toward vindication for the sisters.

“They were held in the Kamsack RCMP Detachment for five days, despite a judge’s order that they be taken to a detention centre away from the detachment,” Innocence Canada wrote in a press release.

Mr. Lockyer has called the Quewezance case, and the fact the sisters are still in custody, an example of fundamental inequities in the justice and correctional systems, and the discrimination that Indigenous people, particularly women, face not only from police and the courts, but also in prison and on parole.

He said he will be applying sometime in the next month for the sisters’ release on bail pending the appeal hearing.
